titulo: Discourse markers to structure formal speech
descripcion_es: Opening, linking the parts, buying time and closing a presentation.
resumen: Expressions that guide the listener through an oral presentation (signposting): introducing the topic and the outline, moving from one part to another, going back, buying time to think and concluding. They are the backbone of the oral language exam.

explicacion.texto: In an oral presentation the listener cannot reread: you have to tell them where you are going, mark each transition and recap. Organise the expressions by function and have two or three of each ready.

filas: I'd like to talk about… / The topic I'm going to address is…
opening and introducing the topic
The topic I'm going to address is the ageing population.
I've divided my presentation into three parts.
announcing the structure
I've divided my presentation into three parts.
First, I'll look at… Then I'll move on to… Finally, I'll…
announcing the outline
First, I'll look at the causes.
Let me start by…
starting
Let me start by defining the term.
Moving on to… / Let's now turn to…
moving on to another part
Let's now turn to the consequences.
This brings me to my next point.
transition
This brings me to my next point: funding.
As I mentioned earlier… / Going back to…
referring back to something
As I mentioned earlier, costs are rising.
I'll come back to this later.
postponing a point
I'll come back to this later on.
Let me put it another way.
rephrasing
Let me put it another way: we can't afford it.
To give you an example… / A case in point is…
giving an example
A case in point is the Irish experience.
It's worth noting / pointing out that…
highlighting
It's worth noting that the data is incomplete.
What I'm trying to say is…
clarifying
What I'm trying to say is that timing matters.
Let me think about that for a moment.
buying time
That's a complex question. Let me think about that for a moment.
How shall I put it?
buying time
How shall I put it? It was a partial success.
That's an interesting question.
buying time (when asked a question)
That's an interesting question; I'd say yes.
To sum up / To recap,
recapping
To recap, there are three main factors.
In conclusion, I would say that…
concluding
In conclusion, I would say that reform is urgent.
The key takeaway is…
main message
The key takeaway is that we must act now.
Thank you for your attention. I'm happy to take any questions.
closing and inviting questions
Thank you for your attention. I'm happy to take any questions.

items: Don't translate Spanish “Voy a hablar sobre” as “I'm going to talk over”: it is “talk about”.
Avoid reading: the expressions let you speak from minimal notes.
To buy time, an expression is better than a long silence or an “er…”.

ejemplos.frase: I've divided my talk into three parts: causes, effects and solutions.
ejemplos.traduccion: He dividido mi exposición en tres partes: causas, efectos y soluciones.

ejemplos.frase: Let's now turn to the role of the European Union.
ejemplos.traduccion: Pasemos ahora al papel de la Unión Europea.

ejemplos.frase: As I mentioned earlier, the data only covers urban areas.
ejemplos.traduccion: Como he mencionado antes, los datos solo abarcan zonas urbanas.

ejemplos.frase: A case in point is the city of Pontevedra, which banned cars from the centre.
ejemplos.traduccion: Un buen ejemplo es Pontevedra, que prohibió los coches en el centro.

ejemplos.frase: It's worth pointing out that these figures are provisional.
ejemplos.traduccion: Conviene señalar que estas cifras son provisionales.

ejemplos.frase: To recap, we have looked at three possible scenarios.
ejemplos.traduccion: Recapitulando, hemos examinado tres posibles escenarios.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I'm going to speak about of the pension system.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I'm going to talk about the pension system.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: In first place, I will analyse the causes.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: First of all, I will analyse the causes.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “En primer lugar”: first, first of all, firstly; “in the first place” exists but is used mainly when arguing.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Now I pass to the second part.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Now I'll move on to the second part.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “Pasar a” is “move on to” or “turn to”.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Thank you for your attention. Do you have any doubt?
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Thank you for your attention. Do you have any questions?
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: To invite questions you say “questions”; “doubt” means doubt in the sense of distrust.

ejercicios.frase: I've ___ my presentation into three parts.
ejercicios.explicacion: The expression in the table for announcing the structure is “I've divided my presentation into three parts”. The key is the verb divide with the preposition into, equivalent to Spanish “dividir en”. The clue is the complement into three parts after the gap: only divided fits with into without adding another preposition. It is one of the most useful opening sentences for the oral exam.
ejercicios.traduccion: He dividido mi presentación en tres partes.

por_opcion.divided: Correct: divide into = Spanish “dividir en”; it is the standard expression for announcing the structure.
por_opcion.split up in: Incorrect: split up means “to separate” (a couple) or “to share out”, and besides, the preposition would be into, not in; split into three parts would be possible.
por_opcion.parted: Incorrect: part means “to separate” or “to say goodbye” (part company), and it is not used for dividing a presentation.
por_opcion.separated of: Incorrect: separate is used with from or into, never with of; it is a calque of Spanish “separar de”.

glosario.definicion_l: the activity of formally presenting something (as a prize or reward) · a show or display; the act of presenting something to sight or view

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with a verb (moving on to another part).
ejercicios.frase: Let's now ___ on to the second part of the talk.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “Moving on to… / Let's now turn to…” for moving on to another part. The key is the phrasal verb move on to: to “move on to” a new point (Spanish “pasar a”). The clue is the particle on to after the gap and the structure Let's + infinitive. Go on to is also accepted because it means “to proceed next to”, although move on to is the most common expression.
ejercicios.traduccion: Pasemos ahora a la segunda parte de la charla.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Pass on to means “to transmit” something to someone; it is the calque of Spanish “pasar a” that the card lists as an error.
Turn to is correct for moving on to another part, but without on: turn on to is not the expression; with on to you need move or go.
Let's is followed by the infinitive without to: move.

glosario.definicion_l: an exchange of ideas via conversation · discussion; (‘talk about’ is a less formal alternative for ‘discussion of’)

ejercicios.frase: Now I pass to the conclusions.
respuestas: Now I'll move on to the conclusions.
Now I'll turn to the conclusions.
Now I move on to the conclusions.
Now I turn to the conclusions.
Now let's move on to the conclusions.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is one of the typical errors listed on the card: Spanish “pasar a” is not pass to, but move on to or turn to. The clue is pass to, a literal calque from Spanish. Several corrections are accepted: with the present or the future (I'll move on to, I move on to), with turn to, or with the invitation Let's move on to.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “pasar a” is “move on to” or “turn to”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Now I pass to the conclusions.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: pass to is a calque; the expression is move on to or turn to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Now I'll pass on to the conclusions.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Pass on to means “to transmit”; to move on to another point you say move on to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Now I'll move to the conclusions.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The particle on is missing: the expression is move on to.

ejercicios.frase: This ___ me to my next point: the cost of the project.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “This brings me to my next point” as a transition expression. The key is bring someone to something: “to take someone to something”, here in a figurative sense. The clue is the structure “This ___ me to my next point”: the subject this (what I have just said) leads me to the next point. It is an elegant transition because it links the two parts logically.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “This brings me to my next point” = this leads me to the next point.
ejercicios.traduccion: Esto me lleva a mi siguiente punto: el coste del proyecto.

por_opcion.brings: Correct: this brings me to my next point is the fixed transition expression.
por_opcion.puts: Incorrect: put means “to place”; “this puts me to” makes no sense in English.
por_opcion.carries: Incorrect: carry means “to take, to transport” physically (carry a bag); it does not form this expression.
por_opcion.makes: Incorrect: make means “to do, to make”; “this makes me to” is not grammatical (make + person takes no to).

glosario.definicion_l: the total spent for goods or services including money and time and labor · the property of having material worth (often indicated by the amount of money something would bring if sold)

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the expression for giving an example.
ejercicios.frase: A case in ___ is the Danish pension system.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “A case in point is…” for giving an example: it means “an illustrative example, a relevant case”. The clue is the expression a case in ___, which is fixed and only allows point. It is more formal than for example and very useful for introducing a specific case in a presentation on economic policy.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “A case in point” = a good example.
ejercicios.traduccion: Un buen ejemplo de ello es el sistema de pensiones danés.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “A case in example” does not exist; the fixed expression is a case in point.
The case in question means “the case being discussed”, with a different structure; the expression for giving an example is a case in point.
In fact means Spanish “de hecho”; a case in fact is not an English expression.

glosario.significado: un buen ejemplo, un caso ilustrativo

ejercicios.enunciado: Choose the correct option to buy time.
ejercicios.frase: That's a tricky question. Let me ___ about that for a moment.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table gives “Let me think about that for a moment” for buying time. The grammatical key is that let is followed by person + infinitive without to. The clue is Let me, which requires the base form of the verb: think. It is much better than a long silence or an “er…” when the examining board asks a difficult question.
ejercicios.traduccion: Es una pregunta complicada. Déjeme pensarlo un momento.

por_opcion.think: Correct: let me + infinitive without to.
por_opcion.thinking: Incorrect: let is not followed by -ing.
por_opcion.to think: Incorrect: after let + person the infinitive has no to.
por_opcion.thought: Incorrect: thought is the past simple or past participle; let requires the base form.

glosario.definicion_l: not to be trusted · having concealed difficulty

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the expression (as I mentioned before).
ejercicios.frase: As I mentioned ___, the survey was carried out in 2024.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “As I mentioned earlier…” for referring back to something said earlier in the presentation. The key is earlier, “before, previously”. The clue is the expression As I mentioned ___: it refers to an earlier moment in the talk itself. Before is also accepted, although earlier is the most common form in this expression.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “As I mentioned earlier” refers back to something said before.
ejercicios.traduccion: Como he mencionado antes, la encuesta se realizó en 2024.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Ago needs an amount of time in front of it (two minutes ago); on its own it cannot end the sentence.
It is redundant and does not fit in a one-word gap; earlier or before is enough.
As mentioned above is used in written texts, not in an oral presentation with I mentioned.

glosario.definicion_l: a detailed critical inspection · short descriptive summary (of events)

ejercicios.frase: Thank you for listening. Are there any doubts?
respuestas: Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?
Thank you for listening. Do you have any questions?
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the typical error listed on the card: to invite questions you say questions, not doubts. The clue is the point in the talk (the end, after thanking the audience): the floor is being opened to questions. In English doubt mainly means doubt in the sense of distrust or uncertainty (I have my doubts about the plan), so “any doubts?” sounds as if the speaker fears not being believed. Do you have any questions? is also fine, and just as common for opening the floor to questions.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Thank you for listening. Are there any doubts?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: doubts suggests distrust; to open the floor you say questions.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Thank you for listening. Is there any question?
errores_previstos.explicacion: The natural expression is in the plural: Are there any questions?

errores_previstos.respuesta: Thank you for listening. Are there any doubt?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Besides keeping the false friend, it breaks the agreement (are there with a singular).

glosario.definicion_l: an instance of questioning · the subject matter at issue

glosario.significado: duda en el sentido de desconfianza o incertidumbre
glosario.definicion_l: the state of being unsure of something · uncertainty about the truth or factuality or existence of something

ejercicios.frase: It's worth ___ out that the figures are only estimates.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “It's worth noting / pointing out that…” for highlighting something. The grammatical key is that be worth is followed by -ing. The clue is It's worth ___ out: the verb is point out (to indicate), in the -ing form. It is a very useful expression for qualifying data in a presentation on economics.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cabe señalar que las cifras son solo estimaciones.

por_opcion.pointing: Correct: it's worth + -ing; point out = to indicate (Spanish “señalar”).
por_opcion.to point: Incorrect: be worth is not followed by to + infinitive.
por_opcion.point: Incorrect: worth cannot be followed by the infinitive without to.
por_opcion.pointed: Incorrect: worth is not followed by a past participle.

glosario.definicion_l: an approximate calculation of quantity or degree or worth · a judgment of the qualities of something or somebody
a diagram or picture illustrating textual material · alternative names for the body of a human being

ejercicios.frase: Let me put it another ___: the plan is too expensive.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “Let me put it another way” for rephrasing. The key is put it, which here means “to express it, to say it”, and another way, “in a different manner”. The clue is the expression Let me put it another ___, which only allows way. It is used to clarify an idea that has not come across clearly, without giving the impression that you made a mistake.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Let me put it another way” = in other words.
ejercicios.traduccion: Dicho de otro modo: el plan es demasiado caro.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Another form” is a calque of Spanish “de otra forma”; the fixed expression is another way.
Manner exists (Spanish “manera”), but the fixed expression is put it another way.
You would say in other words, with a different structure; after put it another only way fits.

glosario.palabra: let me put it another way

ejercicios.frase: To ___, there are three reasons why the policy failed.
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table gives “To sum up / To recap” for recapping. The key is recap, an informal abbreviation of recapitulate. The clue is the structure To ___, followed by a summary of what has been said. The false friend the card points out is resume, which in English means “to start again” (Spanish “reanudar”), not “to summarise” (Spanish “resumir”).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “To recap” = recapitulating; “resume” means to start again (Spanish “reanudar”).
ejercicios.traduccion: Recapitulando, hay tres razones por las que la política fracasó.

por_opcion.resume: Incorrect: resume means “to start again” (resume the meeting); Spanish “resumir” is sum up or summarise.
por_opcion.summary: Incorrect: summary is a noun; you would say in summary, not to summary.
por_opcion.conclude up: Incorrect: conclude takes no particle; you would say to conclude.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with one word (I'll come back to this).
ejercicios.frase: I'll come ___ to this point later.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “I'll come back to this later” for postponing a point. The key is the phrasal verb come back to, “to return to” a topic. The clue is the particle missing between come and to: back indicates the return. It is useful when someone asks a question that will be dealt with in another part of the presentation.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Come back to” = to return to a topic.
ejercicios.traduccion: Volveré sobre este punto más adelante.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Come again to is not the expression; returning to a topic is expressed with back.
Come over means “to come, to drop by someone's house”; it cannot be used for returning to a topic.
Return is a verb; it cannot follow come. You would say I'll return to this point later, with a different structure.

ejercicios.frase: Today I'm going to talk about of youth unemployment.
respuestas: Today I'm going to talk about youth unemployment.
Today I am going to talk about youth unemployment.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the typical error on the card: talk about takes no of. The clue is the sequence about of, which adds the English preposition to the Spanish “de”. In English about already means “about, of” and is enough on its own. The uncontracted form I am is also accepted.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hoy voy a hablar del paro juvenil.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Today I'm going to talk about of youth unemployment.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: talk about takes no of.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Today I'm going to talk of youth unemployment.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Talk of exists, but it is not very natural for introducing a topic; the expression is talk about.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Today I'm going to talk over youth unemployment.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Talk over means “to discuss something with someone”; the card warns about this error: you say talk about.

respuestas: I'm happy to take any questions
ejercicios.explicacion: The second table gives “I'm happy to take any questions” as a closing expression for opening the floor to questions. The key is take questions, “to accept or answer questions”, and the structure be happy to + infinitive, “to be glad to”. The order is subject with verb (I'm), happy, to take and the object any questions.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Closing expression for opening the floor to questions.
ejercicios.traduccion: Con mucho gusto responderé a sus preguntas.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'm happy any questions to take
errores_previstos.explicacion: The object goes after the verb: to take any questions.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'm to take happy any questions
errores_previstos.explicacion: The adjective happy goes directly after I'm, followed by to + infinitive.

glosario.significado: estar encantado de, tener mucho gusto en

ejercicios.frase: Let me start ___ defining what we mean by poverty.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “Let me start by…” for starting. The key is start by + -ing: “to begin by doing something”, that is, the first action you are going to perform. The clue is defining, in -ing, after the gap. Start with is followed by a noun (start with a definition), not by -ing in this sense.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Start by + -ing” = to begin by doing something.
ejercicios.traduccion: Permítanme empezar definiendo qué entendemos por pobreza.

por_opcion.by: Correct: start by + -ing = to begin by doing something.
por_opcion.with: Incorrect: start with takes a noun (start with a definition); with -ing the preposition is by.
por_opcion.for: Incorrect: start for does not have this meaning; it is a calque of Spanish “empezar por”.
por_opcion.to: Incorrect: start to + infinitive would be start to define, “to begin to define”, and it does not take -ing.

glosario.definicion_l: the state of having little or no money and few or no material possessions

descripcion_larga_es: Signposting means the expressions that guide the listener through an oral presentation: introducing the topic and the structure, moving from one part to another, going back, giving examples, buying time and concluding. They are the backbone of the oral language exam in the competitive examination: they let you speak from minimal notes, give order and confidence, and help you avoid common calques such as “I pass to” or “any doubts?”.

contexto.que_es: They are fixed expressions that add no content but signal the structure of the talk: they announce the topic and the outline, mark the transitions, refer back to what has been said, rephrase, give examples, buy time and close the presentation. They work like the headings and punctuation of a written text, but in spoken language.
contexto.por_que_importa: The listener cannot reread, so without these signals they get lost even if the content is good. In the TCEE oral language exam they make the presentation coherent, show command of the language and give you a few seconds to think without awkward silences. Using calques (I pass to, any doubts) makes you sound less natural and can lead to misunderstandings: doubt suggests distrust, not questions.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: They are used at the start of a presentation, at each change of section, when giving an example, when clarifying a poorly expressed idea, when facing a difficult question and at the close, when inviting questions. It is a good idea to have two or three ready for each function. Spanish speakers tend to translate “paso a”, “en primer lugar” or “¿alguna duda?” word for word; the card gives the established English expression.
